title: Desire
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer suggests that true fulfillment and joy come from embracing our deepest desires and longings, rather than trying to suppress or satisfy them. This can involve confronting the pain and suffering that often accompanies these feelings, but ultimately leads to spiritual growth and awakening. By letting go of expectations and complacency, we can tap into a sense of inner peace and awareness that is not dependent on external objects or experiences, but rather on the present moment itself.

sentences.text: Well, this morning I would like to talk about a poem of Thomas Traherne, who is usually classified as one of the English metaphysical poets.
That's probably a bogus category, English metaphysical poets.
He was invented, I learned, by Dr.
Johnson.
He invented the category so that he could complain about those poets.
I always thought, John, that our dear friend Philip Whalen considered himself to be a reincarnation of Dr.
Johnson.
He also loved to complain and was eloquent in his crankiness.
Basically, like a lot of the other so-called metaphysical poets, Traherne was more or less a Christian poet, a Christian mystic.
They don't know too much about him, other than that he was a clergyman in a pretty small church in a small town, and that he died of smallpox before he was 40 in 1674.
He was completely unknown as a poet in his lifetime.
He published virtually nothing.
His poetry was lost for a couple of hundred years, until somebody happened to bump into it in a bookstore, like an obscure manuscript, and thought it was John Donne's poetry.
Later it turned out it wasn't John Donne, it was this unknown person named Thomas Traherne.
And now I think he's pretty famous and well regarded.
His work wasn't published until the 20th century.
Can you imagine that?
Amazing.
So this morning I want to read his poem called Desire.
The way I'll do it is I'll read you the whole poem and then I'll go back in parts and talk about it a little bit.
It's a little bit long, but maybe you can just enjoy it as I read it and let the words wash over you and wash out your ears.
Which is what poems are actually supposed to do.
They're supposed to wash out your ears and open up your sense of what meaning is, and therefore what the world is.
We've all been taught in school that we're supposed to [unclear: "fair it out"], the hidden meaning in the poem.
What's this poem about?
What's it saying?
Like a deciphering job, as if it was in a code.
But really and truly, poems are not about anything at all, and they don't really have hidden meanings, and they cannot be deciphered.
If you had a hidden meaning, why would you write a poem?
Just say what you want to say.
The only reason you'd write a poem is because that is the meaning.
There is no hidden meaning.
So anyway, just relax and let the words wash out your ears.
That's my point.
*Desire.

For giving me desire, an eager thirst, a burning ardent fire, a virgin infant flame, a love with which into the world I came, an inward, hidden, heavenly love, which in my soul did work and move and ever, ever me inflame with restless longing, heavenly avarice that never could be satisfied, that did incessantly a paradise unknown suggest and something undescribed discern and bear me to it, be thy name forever praised by me.*

*My parched and withered bones burnt up did seem, my soul was full of groans, my thoughts [unclear: "extensions were like paces reaches steps they did appear"], they somewhat hotly did pursue, knew that they had not all their due, nor ever quiet were, but made my flesh like hungry, thirsty ground, my heart a deep, profound abyss, and every joy and pleasure a wound, so long as I my blessedness did miss, oh happiness, a famine burns, and all my life to anguish.*

*Where are the silent streams, the living waters, and the glorious beams, the sweet, reviving bowers, the shady groves, the sweet and curious flowers, the springs and trees, the heavenly days, the flowery meads and glorious rays, the gold and silver towers, where are they all?

These poor trees, waters, days and shining beams, fruits, flowers, bowers, shady groves and springs, no joy will yield, no more than silent streams, those are but dead material toys, and cannot make my heavenly joys.*

*Oh love, ye [unclear: "amatees"] and friendships that appear above the skies, ye feasts and living paradise, ye senses, honors and imperial treasures that satisfy all appetites, ye sweet affections, and ye high respects, whatever joys there be in triumphs, whatever stand in amicable sweet society, whatever pleasures are his right hand, ye must before I am divine, in full propriety be mine.

This soaring, sacred thirst, ambassador of bliss, approached first, making a place in me that made me apt to prize and taste and see, for not the objects, but the sense of things doth bliss to our soul's dispense.*

*And make it Lord, like thee, sense, feeling, taste, complacency and sight, these are the true and real joys, the living flowing inward, melting, bright and heavenly pleasures, all the rest are toys, which is founded in desire, as light in flame.
And heat in fire.*
[unclear: "Traversed"] poem on desire.

*For giving me desire, an eager thirst, a burning ardent fire, a virgin infant flame, a love with which into the world I came, an inward hidden heavenly love, which in my soul did work and move, and ever, ever me inflame, with restless longing, heavenly avarice, that never could be satisfied, that did incessantly, a paradise unknown suggest, and something undescribed discern, and bear me to it, be thy name forever praised by me.*
So, this first stanza plainly says, thanks God for giving me desire, I will forever praise your name for that great favor.
But it's funny how he does it, because the first line begins "for giving me desire," and then the last line of this stanza says, "be thy name forever praised by me."
And in between, he is passionately telling us how he experiences desire.
And his description of desire is really wonderful, I think.
"An inward hidden heavenly love" that brought me into the world.
Which is true, right?
We are all brought into the world thanks to desire.
The desire of our parents for one another, or maybe not, maybe just the desire of genes to reproduce themselves on and on into the world.
So we are all born thanks to desire, and yet this poignant desire is very difficult.
It has a lot of bad effects.
It inflames us with restless longing that can never be satisfied.
Heavenly avarice, he calls it, that seeks a paradise that cannot be described or known, and that bears him on toward that impossible unknowable paradise.
So desire is too immense for us, it's too much for us.
I can relate to that, can you?
I think it's true for all of us.
We want this or that, we think we are all very sophisticated, spiritual people, so we don't want a bunch of stuff.
We want inner stuff.
We don't need outer stuff, but the inner stuff.
Desire is endless.
And maybe we can appreciate the illusion that for a moment anyway we satisfy it.
Just long enough so that we can recover and quickly go on to the next thing that we desire.
The fix we seek and seem to satisfy never really fixes us, because what we desire is much, much more than any apparent object.
Whether it's a person that we're desperately, desperately in love with, or some shiny object that we aspire to possess (although really, what is possession?

Do we possess anything really?), or whether we're seeking a heightened experience, whatever it is we think we want, what we really want, what Thomas Traherne definitely really wants, is something absolutely impossible not only to get but even to know what it is.
Our desire is objectless and infinitely restless.
It never ever ends.
And it can seem painful and horrible.
And yet, as he says, praise God for this desire.
It is the most precious thing of all.
*My parched and withered bones burnt up did seem.
My soul was full of groans.* Sorry.
*My thoughts extensions were like paces reaches steps they did appear.
They somewhat hotly did pursue.
Knew that they had not all their due, nor ever quiet were.
But made my flesh like hungry, thirsty ground.
My heart a deep, profound abyss.
And every joy and pleasure so long as I, my blessedness, did miss.
Oh happiness!
A famine burns.
And all my life to languish turns.*
So in this stanza, the blessed, impossible desire that we learned about in the last stanza just gets worse and worse.
The problem is worse and worse.
Maybe you find this hard to relate to, or maybe not.
The withered bones and the groaning soul.
But I bet that we can all relate to the thoughts that are extensions of the groaning soul.
The thoughts that hotly pursue us and we can't get rid of them.
The thoughts that are never satisfied, that go on and on and on.
Yak, yak, yak, yak, yak, yak, yak.
Making our flesh crawl and our hearts sink.
This begins to sound almost like something I hope that nobody in this session is feeling, and I hope that you have never experienced.

Although it is not at all uncommon, especially among religious types like Traherne, this searing, horrible, obsessive, bottomless, dark despair that grabs you and will not let you go, and that turns every joy and pleasure in life into an insult.
Maybe some of you know this feeling.
Terror, terror.
He seems in the poem to be recalling vividly this feeling.
But now he knows its true source.
He was missing the blessedness, the healing faith that only comes through a thoroughgoing confrontation with despair.
And this of course is very Christian, right?
It's a very Christian trope, also in Judaism.
We human beings, so pathetic, so vulnerable.
The truer we see ourselves, the more despair we feel.
Ah, being human, what a catastrophe.
People complain a lot about the judging mind, especially the self-judging mind.
Well, there's a good reason for that self-judging mind.
It's more than just a psychological problem that we can fix with a little positive psychology or something.
It is deeply ingrained in us, deeply ingrained in our Western culture, deeply part of our religious sensibility and a part of our humanness.
We are nothing.
We are no one.
And we know it.
We're less than nothing, less than no one.
No wonder we judge ourselves so harshly.
No wonder we fall into despair.
And in that moment of most profound sorrow, God appears to us and we're saved.
It turns out that our cracked heart is God's opening and our opening to God.
Now this whole process might or might not sound like a good thing to you.
And I think for people for whom it does not sound like a very good thing, Buddhism is very appealing, because it doesn't seem to go into all that.
People like Buddhism and think, thank goodness, I avoid all that, probably.
That's the tricky part.
It looks like it's different, but I'm not so sure how different it is.
It tweaks it a little differently.
But I think that bodhisattvas also suffer great despair.
Bodhisattvas also see the depth of the suffering that is built into the human heart.
As bad as the world might seem to you, as dark as life can feel from time to time, it's way worse than that.
Way, way worse than that.
Very few of us can stand to contemplate the tremendous reservoir of suffering that overflows Alaya Vijnana.
Immense, horrifying, inside and out.
Bodhisattvas contemplate this.
They breathe in and they come to deeply understand its nature.
Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara practices hearing the cries of the world.
She sits and listens and hears the cries of the world, the suffering that is absolutely everywhere.
Her practice is to listen to the sound of the sea, the endless ebbing and flowing, ebbing and flowing, echoing our human pain.
And in this sound she hears the music of emptiness, the point of peace at the heart of the pain.
And all this, remember, is about desire.
It's thanks to desire we feel this pain, and it's thanks to this pain that we awaken.
The Buddha taught four truths.
The first one is that the nature of conditioned existence is suffering.
And the next one is that the cause of suffering is desire.
For bodhisattvas the path isn't the end of suffering and the elimination of desire.
It's understanding desire and embracing suffering.
*Where are the silent streams, the living waters and the glorious beams?
The sweet, reviving bowers, the shady groves, the sweet and curious flowers, the springs, the trees, the heavenly days, the flowery meads and glorious rays, the gold and silver towers?
Alas, all these are poor and empty things.
Trees, waters, days and shining beams, fruits, flowers, bowers, shady groves and springs, no joy will yield no more than silent streams.
Those are but dead material toys and cannot make my heavenly joys.*

So Traherne is telling us about the hollow feeling we sometimes have when we look at beautiful things, at those moments when we're so out of touch with our blessedness, with our intimate selves, that nothing can be beautiful anymore.
And the whole world is dead to us.
And the solace that we might find in natural things is missing.
And the only thing we feel is our endless yearning for something more than what appears before us.

*O Love, ye [unclear: "amatees"] and friendships that appear above the skies, ye feasts and living pleasures, ye senses, honors and imperial treasures that satisfy all appetites, ye sweet affections, and ye high respects, whatever joys there be in triumphs whatsoever,*
*...stand in amicable sweet society, whatever pleasures are at his right hand, ye must, before I am divine, in full propriety be mine.*
I'm a little puzzled by this stanza.
When I've talked about this poem before, I usually leave it out.
If I were Thomas Traherne, I would excise this stanza.
I don't think it helps the poem.
Maybe you like it, maybe it makes sense to you, but it's hard to tell.

He seems to be saying something like, all of a sudden, that love and all instances of love and fellowship among people flow from this desire, and all this will be his, and it must be his as soon as he's close to God.
Maybe he's saying something like that.
Anyway, who knows?
I tried to read it indicating the exclamation point that exists at the end of every phrase of the line.
Thomas Traherne is clearly writing these lines very enthusiastically.
So maybe he's so inspired he himself doesn't know what he means.
Anyway, I thought, out of obligation to the completion of the poem, I would give you that stanza that I would just as soon leave out myself.
The last stanza, though, is really wonderful and very clear, and it gives you the capping of the poem.
*This soaring sacred thirst, ambassador of bliss, approached first, making a place in me that made me apt to prize and taste and see.
For not the objects, but the sense of things doth bliss to our souls dispense, and make it Lord like thee.
Sense, feeling, taste, complacency and sight, these are the true and real joys.
The living, flowing, inward, melting, bright and heavenly pleasures.
All the rest are toys, all which are founded in desire as light in flame and heat in fire.*
So desire, with all of its pain, probably because of all of its pain, is sacred.
It's our teacher and it's an ambassador of bliss, and it makes a place in us of appreciation.
Our wanting this and that, our longing for whatever it is we think we long for that we can never get, is an important practice for us, a beautiful practice.
It blazes a trail into the heart that we need to follow.
And if we go far enough, we'll find what we're really looking for: the real joys, the living, flowing, inward, bright and melting heavenly pleasures.
*For not the object, but the sense of things doth bliss to our souls dispense and make it Lord like thee.*
It isn't what we think we want that we want.
It's the wanting itself.
The sense of things.
What does that mean?
It's not the objects, but the sense of things.
I don't know what that means.
Not the things, the sense of things.
Not other than this world, but the sense of this world.
It's this appreciation of the sense of things that makes our souls blissful and God-like.
When we enter into this sense of things, the nothing in our soul touches the nothing that is God.
Maybe Bodhisattvas call it suchness or thusness, this sense of things.
The song of the bird that isn't the song of the bird and yet is just the song of the bird.
That sound that chimes through the senses and finally, for just this moment, satisfies this endless desire.
So I don't think our practice is very different from Traherne's.
Our longing for transcendence, our knowing that this world is never going to be enough and that everything in it is just a toy, is satisfied only in a moment.
Not elsewhere, but right here.
Really right here.
Desire is flame and fire.
It sears.
It destroys.
And desire is light and warmth at the same time.
Maybe just as an aside, you notice the word "complacency" in there.
Maybe it seems odd to you, the word complacency where he wrote it.
It just shows you how words change their meaning over time.
He's writing hundreds of years ago.
In our time, complacency is kind of a negative thing.
It means you're satisfied enough that you don't get up off your butt and do what you should be doing, complacently.
But the reason you don't get up off your butt is that you're pretty happy with everything.
It's fine.
So complacency actually means pleasure and happiness in things.
He's using it in its original sense.
But like I said, for the last several hundred years we're so obsessed with critiquing everything and making it better that to be pleased with things is a bad thing.
To be pleased, you should be restlessly upset and start another coal plant.
In 1647, it was meant to feel complacency.
It's a pleasure.
[unclear: "The other day was several days ago to the great song of Psalms"] which is the world's greatest of all time love poem, and which includes lines such as the following.
A lot of these love poems are always from the male point of view, but the song of Psalms is both from a male and a female point of view.
Him describing her, her describing him.
*My beloved's head is as the most fine gold.
His locks are curled and black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside water brooks, washed with milk and fitly set.
His cheeks are as a bed of spices, banks of sweet herbs.*
Nice cheeks.
*His lips are like lilies dripping with flowing myrrh.
His legs, pillars of marble set upon sockets of gold.*
Sort of coming from the description of the temple built with sockets of gold.
*And his mouth is most sweet.
He is all together lovely.*
It goes on like that for quite a long time.
Somebody gave me, people gave me a lot of books, and I have stacks of books that I intend to read and now realize that I will die with a reading list.
But anyway, I did read a couple of these books that were given to me.

One was the poems of Salomon Ibn al-Ghabirol and the other one was a biography and poetry of Yehuda al-Levi, who were roughly contemporary Jewish poets during the Spanish, Muslim Spanish diaspora, around the same time as the composition of Omar in the 13th century.
And their poems follow right along from the Song of Songs.
You probably are most familiar with the spirit of them from the poems of the Sufi poet Rumi.
Rumi is in the same sort of spirit: passionate love poems to God.
But they also wrote almost the same poem in a secular context: love poems.
And I learned in reading all this that the tradition in which they were writing spread from Spain to France, where it was taken up by the troubadour poets.
From there it became general in western culture.
So romantic love is actually a concept invented in the 13th century.
It came from the Song of Songs and was flipped over, and then went through Europe, and now we get it.
But the troubadours' idea of romantic love was always sad and tragic.
The whole essence of it was a poetry of longing and sorrow, a desperate reaching out for an impossibly wonderful beloved who could never be possessed.
So this was not Jane Austen, you know; it always ends with marriage.
Doesn't it?
It always ends with longing, and the music of longing.
And I think it might not be too much to say that our popular songs, all the pop songs that you tune in on the radio, are almost always about this romantic love and all the trouble that it brings.

All of our pop songs, the romantic comedies that we go to the movies to see, all the sitcoms on TV, and maybe even as it plays out in our own actual lives, it all comes from, it's invented by, Solomon and Spanish poets and all the European poets that follow them.
This depth of desire and all it means to us has these roots.
So all this stuff about desire and love sounds a little un-Buddhist, right?
You don't think of the Buddha pining away and longing desperately, his unrequited love for a woman or a man or for God.
This doesn't sound like Buddha, right?
And we Buddhists in our quiet zendos seem quite self-contained and sober, even if we sometimes have a sense of humor and a sense of play, like the old Zen masters sometimes did.
But looks can be deceiving.
In fact, Bodhisattvas understand perfectly well this feeling.

Their love for sentient beings and their passionate wish to serve them endlessly, in the glorious, ongoing, spectacular and fabulous failure that is the Bodhisattva commitment, is described by Shantideva in his Bodhikaryavatara, in the chapter on very joyful effort, in this way.
You can't believe that this is Shantideva, in 8th century India, writing this, this good Buddhist.
Shantideva, he says:
*One should be addicted, you should be addicted, solely to the task one is undertaking.
One should be intoxicated by that task, insatiable, like someone hankering for the pleasure and the fruit of love play.
A task is performed for the sake of satisfaction, notwithstanding that there may or may not be satisfaction.*
So this is why we're all paranoid all the time, because everything we do is risky.
When we have an expectation, when we want something, we may get it but we might not.
Everything is a little perilous.
Shantideva goes on: so in other words, a task is performed for the sake of satisfaction, notwithstanding that maybe you will get it or not.
*But how can one for whom the task itself is satisfaction ever be satisfied without a task?*
In other words, it's not at all about results for bodhisattvas, because the bodhisattvas don't care at all what the results are.
That's not where they get their satisfaction.
It's the task itself, the practice itself: to practice and go on practicing for the sake of others endlessly and forever.
That is the satisfaction.
So paradoxically, the only thing that satisfies the bodhisattva is dissatisfaction, to keep on going on and on and on forever.
That's the satisfaction.
That's why I say bodhisattvas are always failures, because they're never going to get to the end of it and say, "Ah, finally I did it, I saved all sentient beings, that was great."
It's not going to happen.
So bodhisattvas are by definition holy failures.
Shantideva goes on:
*One cannot get enough of the pleasures of cyclical existence.
They're like honey on a razor's edge.*
This is, like Traherne is saying, these things are mere toys only.
They're painful toys; they're sweet but painful.
So you can't get enough.
That's what worldly pleasures are: you can't get enough of them.
*But how could you ever get enough of the benign, ambrosial acts of merit, always sweet?*
Desire is a part of the bodhisattva path: desire turned just enough to be the same energy that we're born with and out of which we're born, and yet at the same time something very different.
Traherne's most famous work is called *Centuries of Meditations*.
These seem to be short paragraphs that he wrote, I'm guessing, as a practice.
You could do this yourself every day: write a short paragraph, a devotional paragraph.
And they're called centuries because he would write a hundred, and he would say, "Now I have a century," and then he would write another century.
So there are many, many centuries of meditations.
Number thirty of the first century:

*Till your spirit filleth the whole world, and the stars are your jewels; till you are as familiar with the ways of God in all ages as with your walk and table; till you are intimately acquainted with that shady nothing out of which the world was made; till you love men so as to desire their happiness with a thirst equal to the zeal of your own; till you delight in God for being good to all; till you feel all that you never enjoy the world; till you more feel than your private estate and are more present in the hemisphere, considering the glories and the beauties there, than in your own house; till you remember how lately you were made, and how wonderful it was when you came into this world, and more rejoice in the palace of your glory than if it had been made but this morning.*
So, being human, what a fabulous possibility.
So please continue your sitting, but now maybe you can add, from today, this spirit of searching and seeking and reaching out for the beloved endlessly.
And this is living in vow, and this is our peaceful life.
